content: Shock is a clinical syndrome characterized by circulatory failure, leading to inadequate cellular oxygen utilization. Its diagnosis relies on clinical signs and biochemical abnormalities indicative of tissue hypoperfusion. Shock is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate treatment, regardless of the underlying cause. Common Causes of Shock: Cardiogenic Shock: Arrhythmic Causes: Sinoatrial block, atrioventricular block, ventricular tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia. Mechanical Causes: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, acute mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal defect. Myopathic Causes: Cardiomyopathy, myocardial contusion, myocardial infarction, myocarditis, post-ischemic myocardial stunning, septic myocardial depression, hypothyroidism. Pharmacologic Causes: Anthracyclines, calcium channel blockers. Obstructive Shock: Decreased Cardiac Compliance: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis. Decreased Ventricular Preload: Intrathoracic tumor, mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), tension pneumothorax. Increased Ventricular Afterload: Aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, acute pulmonary hypertension. Hypovolemic Shock: Fluid Depletion: Dehydration, diarrhea, extensive burns, polyuria, vomiting, third spacing (e.g., endometritis, pancreatitis, peritonitis, pleural effusions). Hemorrhage: Ectopic pregnancy, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforated peptic ulcer, post-procedural or post-surgical bleeding, retroperitoneal hemorrhage, ruptured ovarian cyst, trauma. Distributive Shock: Sepsis: Including toxic shock syndrome. Anaphylactic or Anaphylactoid Reactions. Neurogenic Shock. Adrenal Crisis. Focused Initial Rapid Evaluation (FIRE): A focused initial rapid evaluation should be performed to identify patients requiring immediate intervention. Urgent management is necessary for critical cases. Complete Diagnostic Approach: History: Review all medications, as antihypertensives can cause significant hypotension, especially in volume depletion or over-diuresis. Consider anaphylaxis if a new drug was recently started and the patient presents with respiratory distress. Accompanying symptoms that may help identify the underlying disease include abdominal pain, chest discomfort, diarrhea, dyspnea, hematemesis, hematochezia, polydipsia, polyuria, and vomiting. Physical Examination: Vital Signs: Fever may suggest sepsis or anaphylaxis related to transfusion. Hypothermia may indicate sepsis, adrenal crisis, or myxedema. Bradycardia or tachycardia can be primary or secondary processes. Pulsus paradoxus may occur in cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, or tension pneumothorax. Pulsus alternans may be seen in heart failure, severe aortic insufficiency, or hypovolemic shock. Tachypnea is common in pneumothorax, sepsis, and cardiogenic shock. Hypopnea may indicate narcotic or sedative overdose. Confirm arterial hypotension by manually checking blood pressure in both arms. Consider arterial line placement. Postural hypotension suggests volume depletion or autonomic dysfunction but should not be tested in hypotensive patients. Mental Status: Altered mental status may indicate inadequate perfusion to vital organs or the use of sedatives or narcotics. Cutaneous Findings: Decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes indicate dehydration. Cool extremities, clammy and mottled skin, peripheral cyanosis, and delayed capillary refill are common in cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock. Warm, moist skin may represent the hyperdynamic phase of septic shock. Extensive burns and severe trauma may be evident and associated with significant fluid loss. Hyperpigmentation may indicate adrenal crisis. Neck: Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) correlates with increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) and decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). Jugular venous distention or elevated JVP typically occurs in heart failure, tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, superior vena cava obstruction, constrictive pericarditis, or cardiac tamponade. Kussmaul's sign (elevated JVP during inspiration) may be seen in constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, tricuspid stenosis, superior vena cava obstruction, or right ventricular infarction. A positive abdominojugular reflux correlates with a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of 15 mmHg or greater and may be seen in cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, tricuspid insufficiency, inferior vena cava obstruction, or heart failure. Cardiovascular: A decrescendo early systolic murmur may indicate acute severe mitral regurgitation. A third heart sound (S3) is associated with heart failure. A pansystolic murmur along the lower left sternal border with a palpable thrill suggests a ventricular septal defect. Pericardial friction rubs are indicative of pericarditis. Distant, muffled heart sounds may indicate cardiac tamponade. Pulmonary: Tracheal deviation may suggest tension pneumothorax. Stridor and wheezing may indicate anaphylaxis or acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Rales may be present in anaphylaxis, pneumonia, or heart failure. Chest percussion may aid in diagnosing tension pneumothorax, pleural effusions, or pneumonia. Abdominal: Ecchymoses may indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Hepatomegaly may be associated with inferior vena cava obstruction or heart failure. Rebound tenderness with absent bowel sounds may suggest sepsis due to intra-abdominal infection, ischemic colitis, or gastrointestinal hemorrhage. A pulsatile mass may indicate an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Rectal: Bright red blood or melena suggests gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Diminished sphincter tone may indicate spinal cord injury. Extremities: Digital clubbing and edema may indicate heart failure. Erythema at the site of venous access may suggest catheter-associated infection. Pelvic girdle pain or instability may indicate a pelvic fracture. Genitals: Perform a pelvic examination in women of childbearing age to rule out ectopic pregnancy or pelvic inflammatory disease. Neurologic: Agitation or delirium may indicate poor cerebral perfusion. Meningeal signs may suggest meningitis. Laboratory Findings: Complete Blood Count: Hemoglobin and hematocrit levels may remain normal in acute blood loss until volume is replenished. Leukocytosis with or without a left shift of neutrophils suggests sepsis. Thrombocytopenia with coagulation abnormalities indicates disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a potential complication of sepsis. Electrolytes: Decreased bicarbonate levels may indicate metabolic acidosis or compensatory respiratory alkalosis. Hyperkalemia due to transcellular shift is commonly associated with metabolic acidosis. Coagulation Panel: Abnormalities may result from DIC, over-anticoagulation, or hepatic failure. Cardiac Markers: Elevated troponin and CK-MB levels suggest myocardial infarction but may also have extracardiac etiologies. Liver Function: Elevated conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and hepatic aminotransferases are typical in ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) due to cardiogenic shock. Renal Function: Prerenal azotemia and/or acute tubular necrosis may occur in hypovolemia or reduced cardiac output. Lactate: Hyperlactatemia reflects anaerobic metabolism in hypoperfused tissue and/or impaired hepatic clearance. Effective therapy may reduce lactate levels within hours. Arterial Blood Gas: Lactic acidosis indicates tissue hypoperfusion, commonly seen in septic shock. Severe acidosis may blunt vasopressor effectiveness and increase the risk of arrhythmias. Cultures: Blood, urine, and/or sputum samples should be sent for culture before administering antibiotics if sepsis is suspected. Nasogastric Aspirate: A negative aspirate does not rule out upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Pregnancy Test: Perform in hypotensive women of childbearing age presenting with lower abdominal pain. ECG Findings: ST segment elevation or depression, pathologic Q waves, and hyperacute or negative T waves suggest myocardial infarction or ischemia. Sinus tachycardia with an S1Q3T3 pattern suggests acute pulmonary embolism. Low QRS voltage with electrical alternans indicates cardiac tamponade. QS deflections in precordial leads with right axis deviation and low QRS voltage suggest pneumothorax. Bradyarrhythmias or tachyarrhythmias may also be present. Radiographic Findings: Chest radiographs may help diagnose aortic dissection, cardiac tamponade, pneumonia complicating septic shock, pulmonary edema complicating cardiogenic shock, or tension pneumothorax. CT scans may guide management in cases of occult internal hemorrhage or pulmonary embolism. Hemodynamic Profiles and Echocardiography Findings: Resuscitation should begin while investigating the cause of shock. Correct the underlying cause immediately once identified. Establish venous access via large-bore peripheral lines or a central venous line. Place a Foley catheter to monitor urine output. Obtain blood, urine, and/or sputum cultures before administering antibiotics when sepsis is suspected. Key Considerations: Do not test orthostatic hypotension in hypotensive patients. Do not rely solely on pulse oximeter oxygen saturation readings to assess oxygenation status.
